stem: A 60-year-old man who farmed outdoors for decades has a slowly enlarging dome-shaped, shiny pink nodule on the side of his nose, with a rolled border and fine surface vessels. It is not scaly and has never bled. He has a shave biopsy.
oneliner: 60M + outdoor worker + pearly nodule on nose + rolled edge + telangiectasias → which biopsy feature?

options.A: Atypical squamous cells with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls
options.B: Atypical pigment-producing cells nesting at the dermal-epidermal junction
options.C: Basaloid nests with a palisaded outer row and stromal clefts
options.D: Plump spindle cells lining slit-like vascular spaces
options.E: Basaloid squamous cells with keratin-filled horn cysts

whyNot.A: **Keratin pearls** mean squamous cell carcinoma: scaly, crusted or ulcerated rather than pearly
whyNot.B: **Melanoma** is pigmented and irregular; this nodule is pink and translucent
whyNot.D: **Kaposi sarcoma** forms purple patches or nodules; this nodule is pink and pearly
whyNot.E: **Horn cysts** mean seborrheic keratosis, a brown, waxy, stuck-on plaque, not a pearly pink nodule

why: **Basal cell carcinoma** is the commonest skin cancer, on sun-exposed skin, with a **pearly nodule, rolled edge and telangiectasias**. Tumor islands show **peripheral palisading** and **retraction clefts**; it rarely metastasizes.

idea.rule: Pearly nodule on the face with palisading basaloid nests is basal cell carcinoma.
also: Hedgehog (PTCH1) pathway activation is the driver
Gorlin syndrome gives many basal cell carcinomas

stem: A 35-year-old woman has fever, painful mouth and eye erosions, and sheets of skin that slough with light rubbing ten days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection. More than a third of her body surface has detached. A skin biopsy is examined under the microscope.
oneliner: 35F + fever, mouth and eye erosions + sheets of skin sloughing 10 days after trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole + over 30% body surface detached → which biopsy finding?
ask: Which biopsy finding is most likely?

options.A: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with sparse inflammation
options.B: Suprabasal clefts with 'tombstone' basal cells on the floor
options.C: Split in the granular layer with viable keratinocytes beneath
options.D: Neutrophil microabscesses in the tips of the dermal papillae
options.E: Subepidermal blister rich in eosinophils, epidermis intact

whyNot.B: That cleft is **pemphigus vulgaris**, a chronic autoimmune disease; she has **fever and sheet-like sloughing ten days after a new drug**
whyNot.C: That is **SSSS**, a thin superficial peel with **no mucosal disease**; she has **mouth and eye erosions**
whyNot.D: That is **dermatitis herpetiformis**, with itchy grouped vesicles; she has **painful mucosal erosions and sloughing after a new drug**
whyNot.E: That is **bullous pemphigoid**, a chronic itchy disease of the elderly; she is **35** with acute sloughing and **mucosal erosions** after a sulfonamide

answer: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal detachment and a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate
why: **Sulfonamide exposure 1-2 weeks earlier, mucosal erosions and more than 30% detachment** define **toxic epidermal necrolysis**. Cytotoxic T cells and granulysin kill keratinocytes, so the **entire epidermis is necrotic**, lifts off at the dermoepidermal junction, and the dermis shows only a **thin lymphocytic infiltrate**.

idea.rule: SJS/TEN is a drug-triggered T-cell attack on keratinocytes: dead epidermis, sparse inflammation, mucosa involved.
also: Common triggers: sulfonamides, allopurinol, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, nevirapine
SJS is under 10% and TEN over 30% body surface
